notes: Nine original AQA-style Energetics questions targeting reported gaps: 100 kPa/stated temperature and standard state definitions; ∆H = −q/(1000n) with sign and stoichiometric denominator; formation vs combustion Hess cycles with coefficients; reverse/multiply Hess equations; changed vs unchanged bonds; RP2 temperature-time and uncertainty; practical evaluation. Not official past-paper questions. The calorimetry examples are hypothetical calculations, not experimental procedures.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: (a) State the pressure and temperature rule for standard enthalpy values. (b) Explain the role of standard states. (c) Define standard enthalpy of formation and combustion. (d) Write the standard formation equation for Al₂O₃(s), including states. [7 marks]
markPoints: Standard enthalpy values use 100 kPa pressure.
A standard enthalpy change is given at a stated temperature; 298 K is common, not compulsory.
Substances are in their standard states at the specified conditions.
Standard formation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound is made.
The compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
Standard combustion enthalpy involves complete burning of exactly one mole of substance in oxygen at standard conditions.
The correct one-mole standard formation equation is 2Al(s)+3/2O₂(g)→Al₂O₃(s).
questions.modelAnswer: Standard enthalpy values use 100 kPa pressure. A standard enthalpy change is given at a stated temperature; 298 K is common, not compulsory. Substances are in their standard states at the specified conditions. Standard formation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound is made. The compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions. Standard combustion enthalpy involves complete burning of exactly one mole of substance in oxygen at standard conditions. The correct one-mole standard formation equation is 2Al(s)+3/2O₂(g)→Al₂O₃(s).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: In a calorimetry exercise, 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ reacts with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. H₂SO₄(aq)+2NaOH(aq)→Na₂SO₄(aq)+2H₂O(l). Temperature rises 5.0°C. Assume density 1.00 g cm⁻³, c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and negligible heat lost. Calculate (i) q_solution, (ii) ΔH per mole of reaction as written, and (iii) ΔH per mole of water formed. Show clearly when the coefficient 2 is used. [9 marks]
markPoints: Total solution volume is 25.0+50.0=75.0 cm³.
Mass of the solution is 75.0 g from density 1.00 g cm⁻³.
q_solution=1.5675 kJ.
Amount H₂SO₄=1.00×0.0250=0.0250 mol.
Amount NaOH=1.00×0.0500=0.0500 mol and the 1:2 mole ratio is exact.
Amount of reaction as written =0.0250 mol (the acid's coefficient is 1).
ΔH for one mole of the equation is −1.5675/0.0250=−62.7 kJ mol⁻¹.
Two moles of water form per mole of equation, so ΔH per mole of water formed is −62.7/2=−31.4 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Total solution volume is 25.0+50.0=75.0 cm³. Mass of the solution is 75.0 g from density 1.00 g cm⁻³. q_solution=mcΔT=75.0×4.18×5.0=1567.5 J. q_solution=1.5675 kJ. Amount H₂SO₄=1.00×0.0250=0.0250 mol. Amount NaOH=1.00×0.0500=0.0500 mol and the 1:2 mole ratio is exact. Amount of reaction as written =0.0250 mol (the acid's coefficient is 1). ΔH for one mole of the equation is −1.5675/0.0250=−62.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Two moles of water form per mole of equation, so ΔH per mole of water formed is −62.7/2=−31.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: For 2CO(g)+O₂(g)→2CO₂(g), use these ΔfH° values in kJ mol⁻¹: CO(g)=−110.5, CO₂(g)=−393.5, O₂(g)=0. (a) Calculate ΔH° for the reaction as written. (b) State ΔH per mole of CO₂ produced. Explain precisely where the stoichiometric coefficients are used. [6 marks]
markPoints: Use ΔHreaction=ΣΔfH°(products)−ΣΔfH°(reactants).
Multiply CO₂ formation enthalpy by 2, giving 2×(−393.5)=−787.0 kJ.
Multiply CO formation enthalpy by 2, giving 2×(−110.5)=−221.0 kJ.
Elemental O₂(g) is in its standard state, so its ΔfH° is zero.
Reaction ΔH=−787.0−(−221.0)=−566.0 kJ for the equation as written.
The reaction produces 2 mol CO₂, so enthalpy per mol of CO₂ produced is −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Use ΔHreaction=ΣΔfH°(products)−ΣΔfH°(reactants). Multiply CO₂ formation enthalpy by 2, giving 2×(−393.5)=−787.0 kJ. Multiply CO formation enthalpy by 2, giving 2×(−110.5)=−221.0 kJ. Elemental O₂(g) is in its standard state, so its ΔfH° is zero. Reaction ΔH=−787.0−(−221.0)=−566.0 kJ for the equation as written. The reaction produces 2 mol CO₂, so enthalpy per mol of CO₂ produced is −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Use these standard enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹): C(s, graphite)=−393.5 and CO(g)=−283.0. Calculate ΔH for 2C(s)+O₂(g)→2CO(g). Explain why combustion-cycle arrows need the reactants-minus-products rule and calculate enthalpy per mole CO formed. [6 marks]
markPoints: Both carbon and carbon monoxide can combust to the common final products CO₂(g).
Use the combustion Hess rule: sum of reactant combustion enthalpies minus sum of product combustion enthalpies.
Reactant combustion sum is 2×(−393.5)=−787.0 kJ.
Product combustion sum is 2×(−283.0)=−566.0 kJ.
Dividing by two gives −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹ per mole CO formed.
questions.modelAnswer: Both carbon and carbon monoxide can combust to the common final products CO₂(g). Use the combustion Hess rule: sum of reactant combustion enthalpies minus sum of product combustion enthalpies. Reactant combustion sum is 2×(−393.5)=−787.0 kJ. Product combustion sum is 2×(−283.0)=−566.0 kJ. ΔH=−787.0−(−566.0)=−221.0 kJ for 2C(s)+O₂(g)→2CO(g). Dividing by two gives −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹ per mole CO formed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Given (1) H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(g), ΔH=−184 kJ; and (2) HCl(g)→HCl(aq), ΔH=−74.8 kJ for one mole HCl. Use Hess's law to calculate ΔH for 2HCl(aq)→H₂(g)+Cl₂(g). Explain when to multiply an equation and when to reverse the sign. [6 marks]
markPoints: The target is the reverse of H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(aq), so its total enthalpy sign must reverse.
The first step H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(g) has ΔH=−184 kJ.
The solution step HCl(g)→HCl(aq) is −74.8 kJ per mole HCl and must be multiplied by 2.
Forward total is −184−149.6=−333.6 kJ.
Reversing the overall equation yields 2HCl(aq)→H₂(g)+Cl₂(g), ΔH=+333.6 kJ.
questions.modelAnswer: The target is the reverse of H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(aq), so its total enthalpy sign must reverse. The first step H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(g) has ΔH=−184 kJ. The solution step HCl(g)→HCl(aq) is −74.8 kJ per mole HCl and must be multiplied by 2. For 2HCl(g)→2HCl(aq), ΔH=2×(−74.8)=−149.6 kJ. Forward total is −184−149.6=−333.6 kJ. Reversing the overall equation yields 2HCl(aq)→H₂(g)+Cl₂(g), ΔH=+333.6 kJ.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Estimate ΔH for ethene hydrogenation C₂H₄(g)+H₂(g)→C₂H₆(g). Mean gas-phase bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C=C 612; C–C 347; H–H 436; C–H 413. Show what bonds change, why unchanged bonds cancel, and how the 2 new C–H bonds affect the calculation. [7 marks]
markPoints: Reaction is C₂H₄(g)+H₂(g)→C₂H₆(g); the four C–H bonds already in ethene are retained.
A C=C bond is broken, using 612 kJ mol⁻¹.
An H–H bond is broken, using 436 kJ mol⁻¹.
A C–C bond forms, releasing magnitude 347 kJ mol⁻¹.
Two new C–H bonds form, releasing magnitude 2×413=826 kJ mol⁻¹.
The two new C–H bonds arise from the change in structure, whereas unchanged bonds cancel; do not multiply an entire bond energy by the number of carbon atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction is C₂H₄(g)+H₂(g)→C₂H₆(g); the four C–H bonds already in ethene are retained. A C=C bond is broken, using 612 kJ mol⁻¹. An H–H bond is broken, using 436 kJ mol⁻¹. A C–C bond forms, releasing magnitude 347 kJ mol⁻¹. Two new C–H bonds form, releasing magnitude 2×413=826 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH estimate = (612+436)−(347+826)=−125 kJ mol⁻¹. The two new C–H bonds arise from the change in structure, whereas unchanged bonds cancel; do not multiply an entire bond energy by the number of carbon atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: In an RP2 calorimetry question, initial temperature is 21.0°C and reagents are combined at t=90 s. Cooling readings: t=150 s, 29.2°C; 210 s, 28.8°C; 270 s, 28.4°C. Assume 50.0 g solution, c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, 0.0250 mol of reaction and each thermometer reading ±0.1°C. (a) Extrapolate to t=90 s; (b) calculate corrected ΔT and ΔH; (c) explain why using 29.2°C underestimates magnitude; (d) find % temperature-change uncertainty. [9 marks]
markPoints: The temperature decreases by 0.4°C in each 60-second cooling interval.
Extrapolation from t=150 s back to mixing at t=90 s gives estimated T=29.6°C.
Corrected ΔT=29.6−21.0=8.6°C.
Convert q_solution to 1.7974 kJ.
Moles reacting=0.0250 mol, so ΔH=−1.7974/0.0250=−71.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Direct use of 29.2°C gives too small a rise because the solution has already cooled.
Two temperature measurements each with ±0.1°C uncertainty give absolute ΔT uncertainty ±0.2°C.
Percentage uncertainty in corrected ΔT is (0.2/8.6)×100=2.3%.
questions.modelAnswer: The temperature decreases by 0.4°C in each 60-second cooling interval. Extrapolation from t=150 s back to mixing at t=90 s gives estimated T=29.6°C. Corrected ΔT=29.6−21.0=8.6°C. q_solution=50.0×4.18×8.6=1797.4 J. Convert q_solution to 1.7974 kJ. Moles reacting=0.0250 mol, so ΔH=−1.7974/0.0250=−71.9 kJ mol⁻¹. Direct use of 29.2°C gives too small a rise because the solution has already cooled. Two temperature measurements each with ±0.1°C uncertainty give absolute ΔT uncertainty ±0.2°C. Percentage uncertainty in corrected ΔT is (0.2/8.6)×100=2.3%.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: You may be asked about AQA Required Practical 2 even when your mock is not Paper 3. State what the polystyrene cup and lid are for, what temperature readings are needed, why a cooling graph is extrapolated, and two sources of systematic underestimation in an exothermic calorimetry result. [6 marks]
markPoints: Polystyrene cup insulates the solution and reduces heat transfer with the external surroundings.
A lid limits heat exchange and reduces evaporation.
Measure the initial temperature of the reagents and the temperature change after reaction using a thermometer/probe.
Extrapolating the subsequent cooling trend to the time of mixing can correct for heat lost during measurement.
Heat loss in an exothermic experiment decreases the measured temperature rise and makes the estimated ΔH less negative.
Heat absorbed by the calorimeter apparatus may not be included in q_solution=mcΔT, causing underestimation of the reaction heat magnitude.
questions.modelAnswer: Polystyrene cup insulates the solution and reduces heat transfer with the external surroundings. A lid limits heat exchange and reduces evaporation. Measure the initial temperature of the reagents and the temperature change after reaction using a thermometer/probe. Extrapolating the subsequent cooling trend to the time of mixing can correct for heat lost during measurement. Heat loss in an exothermic experiment decreases the measured temperature rise and makes the estimated ΔH less negative. Heat absorbed by the calorimeter apparatus may not be included in q_solution=mcΔT, causing underestimation of the reaction heat magnitude.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: For the hypothetical reaction 2H₂(g)+O₂(g)→2H₂O(g), 0.100 mol H₂ reacts completely. An independent calorimetry experiment measures the solution's temperature change. Explain (a) whether to multiply the measured solution mass by 2 in q=mcΔT, (b) the moles of reaction as written, (c) the moles of H₂O formed, (d) which n is used for ΔH per mole reaction versus per mole water, and (e) the number of each bond type counted in a bond enthalpy calculation for the balanced equation. No numerical heat calculation is needed. [6 marks]
markPoints: In q=mcΔT, mass m is the measured mass of the solution; it is not multiplied by a chemical-equation coefficient.
For 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, 0.100 mol H₂ corresponds to 0.0500 mol of reaction as written.
The same amount of H₂ makes 0.100 mol H₂O given complete reaction and the 2:2 ratio.
When ΔH is required per mole of reaction as written, divide reaction heat magnitude by 0.0500 mol.
When ΔH is required per mole of water, divide reaction heat magnitude by 0.100 mol.
To calculate bond enthalpy for the full 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O equation, count 2 H–H bonds broken, 1 O=O bond broken and 4 O–H bonds formed.
questions.modelAnswer: In q=mcΔT, mass m is the measured mass of the solution; it is not multiplied by a chemical-equation coefficient. For 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, 0.100 mol H₂ corresponds to 0.0500 mol of reaction as written. The same amount of H₂ makes 0.100 mol H₂O given complete reaction and the 2:2 ratio. When ΔH is required per mole of reaction as written, divide reaction heat magnitude by 0.0500 mol. When ΔH is required per mole of water, divide reaction heat magnitude by 0.100 mol. To calculate bond enthalpy for the full 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O equation, count 2 H–H bonds broken, 1 O=O bond broken and 4 O–H bonds formed.
